episodes.title: Reality Fracture Common + Uncommon Set Review
Reality Fracture Rare + Mythic Set Review
#872: Reality Fracture Set Review, Commons and Uncommons

synthesis.overview:
Reality Fracture is a dense, synergy-heavy set built around Empower Jace. That mechanic creates or loads a Jace token with -1 surveil 1 and -3 draw a card. Ten two-color archetypes sit on top of it: five allied 'schools' on rails, each with its own shared prepared spell, and five looser enemy pairs. Packs carry fewer commons plus mirrored legend pairs, so decks are uncommon- and rare-heavy. Both Limited Level-Ups (Marc and Alex) and Limited Resources (Marshall and Luis) call the gold cards and charms pushed.

The experts expect a deep format where skill matters: attacking or ignoring Jace tokens, sequencing surveils, and managing a graveyard. Only Level-Ups' rare review reflects some early play, and it describes long, grindy games decided by removal, mana sinks and top-end threats.

The site's simulation (800 bot decks, 100,000 games, average drawn-card win rate 51.8%) broadly agrees that green and red are the places to be. It disagrees sharply on blue, and it is lukewarm on the heavily synergistic schools. Its clearest message is simple: big, sturdy bodies and clean removal win, while tricks, charms and build-arounds underdeliver, at least in bot hands.
synthesis.speed: The experts split here. Level-Ups sees a midrange-to-grindy format with few good aggressive two-drops, and after playing, games decided on turn six or later with frequent board stalls. Limited Resources instead said games tend to be fast and that high-roll starts win. The simulation leans toward Level-Ups: expensive, durable threats post the best numbers, including Bestial Incursion at 59.7%, Ghalta the Unstoppable at 59.5% and Craftwork Crusher at 58.7%. Cheap pump tricks crater. Plan for a slower format, but still run enough early creatures to pressure Jace tokens.
consensus: Empower Jace defines the format. Roughly, Empower 3 is worth about a card, and choosing when to attack a Jace token versus the opponent's face is a core skill.
The gold uncommons are pushed. Craftwork Crusher (A- and B/B+) and Twisted Fates (B and A-) are premium on both shows, and the simulation agrees at 58.7% and 57.5%.
Kiora of Fire and Ashes is a top uncommon (B+/B on both shows), and at 61.9% it is the sim's second-best card overall.
Black and red are rich in efficient removal: Last Gasp, Multiply by Zero, No Admittance, Wrath of the Bloodmane, Fulminous Forte and Extended Absence. Cheap removal that trades up is premium.
Triple-pipped gold cards like Twisted Fates, Hapatra and Craftwork Crusher are meant for their pair, not for splashing.
The color-hate cycle (Essence Burn, Refute Destiny, Terminal Criticism, Precise Redaction, Flourishing Grapple) is sideboard-only in best-of-three.
BG's advertised deathtouch-plus-trample theme looks thin. The sim backs this: Ferocity of the Hunt wins just 42.9%.
Obvious chaff includes both Yargles, Hexhaven Dueling Arena, Perfected Theory and Sphinx's Approach.
debates: Speed: Level-Ups calls the format slow and grindy, while Limited Resources expected fast games where high rolls matter.

Best archetype: Level-Ups' common/uncommon review floated WU flyers as possibly the strongest, and Marc's early pick was RG. Limited Resources doubts that three-mana Heartwood ramp pays off without strong payoffs.
BR pinging: Level-Ups calls it the most dubious archetype and grades Stingerquill Voxmancer C-/D+. Limited Resources calls the deck scary and gives Voxmancer and Grim Repriser B.
Bloombrute: Limited Resources rates it an easily-supported A-, Alex on Level-Ups has it at B-, and Marc gives only C because lifegain enablers are thinner than they look.
Big green legends: Limited Resources has Ghalta the Unstoppable at B- and Titanbones at B, while Level-Ups sits at C-/D+ and D/C-.
Blue interaction: Level-Ups rates Unsummon B- as one of the best commons and Countersculpt B. Limited Resources has both at C.
Surgical Precision: Level-Ups' first impressions predicted one of the best commons (later C+/B-), while Limited Resources gives it C.
Kiora of Salt and Sand: Marc calls the 8/8 plan a trap (C-), while Limited Resources grades it a build-around B.
Mabel, Valley Hero: Limited Resources has it at B+ as a must-kill, while Marc sees a 1/2 that grows itself (C).

colors.take: Level-Ups praises green's strong uncommons and ramp payoffs, and the simulation makes it the best color. Green pairs post 53.2% (RG), 50.8% (BG), 49.9% (UG) and 49.1% (WG). Its commons overperform: Bestial Incursion at 59.7%, Wrecking Gecko at 56.9% and Greenhouse Propagator at 56.2%. The Heartwood enablers themselves are only middling, such as Heartwood Crafter at 50.3% and Konstrari Improviser at 52.0%.

Level-Ups found red better than expected thanks to removal and top end, and the sim agrees. Kiora of Fire and Ashes wins 61.9%, Fulminous Forte 55.0%, Heartstring Puller 55.9%, Tether Technician 54.9%, Awaken the Inferno 54.6% and No Admittance 53.8%. Red sits in three of the four best-performing pairs.

Level-Ups narrowly calls black the worst color but a great support color, and Limited Resources stresses its removal. The sim treats black as solid in BR and BG, with Extended Absence at 56.1% and Multiply by Zero at 54.2%. Its sacrifice and self-mill pieces flop: Winter, Tormented Loner wins 39.1% and Edgar, Ancient Bloodlord 45.1%.

Level-Ups ranks white second-worst, and the sim quietly agrees: every white pair lands between 49.1% and 49.9%. White's best cards are sturdy bodies rather than synergy. Thalia, the Survivor wins 60.7%, Blossom-Blessed Angel 59.5% and Lyra, Archangel of Dawn 58.5%.

This is the biggest split. Level-Ups calls blue possibly the best color at common and uncommon, but in the sim blue pairs run from 45.7% to 50.5%. Its interaction and rares underperform: Unsummon wins 47.9%, Countersculpt 49.6%, Sphinx of False Conclusions 48.3% and Seasoned Cryomancer 46.9%. Bots are likely weakest with flash, counters and library manipulation, so the experts have the better case on blue's ceiling. Still, don't assume blue is the best seat.

pairs.experts: This is Konstrari's Heartwood ramp deck. Marc called it his early favorite for best pair, and Craftwork Crusher is a consensus premium payoff. Limited Resources doubts the ramp pieces and says viability hinges on payoff quality.
pairs.sim: RG is the top pair at 53.2% on a 12% share. The wins come from payoffs and big bodies: Crusher at 58.7%, Bestial Incursion at 59.7% and Ghalta at 59.5%. Enablers like Heartwood Crafter (50.3%) and Woodwork Prodigy (50.8%) are average, which matches Limited Resources' framing.

pairs.experts: This is Stingerquill's non-combat pinging deck. Level-Ups finds it the most dubious archetype, better built grindy around Command the Stage, while Limited Resources thinks it looks scary.
pairs.sim: BR is second at 51.0% but drafted only 5% of the time, so it looks like an open lane. The standouts are sticky bodies and spells rather than pingers: Screeching Soulbreaker at 55.6% and Stingcaster Mage at 55.7%, against Voxmancer at 52.5% and Stingerquill Charm at 51.2%.

pairs.experts: Both shows see a graveyard midrange deck carried by Hapatra, the Desert Fang and Primal Witchstalker. The deathtouch-trample theme is considered thin.
pairs.sim: BG is solid at 50.8%. Carnivorous Cultivator (57.8%) and Vraska, the Cutting Glare (58.3%) lead, while Hapatra (52.1%) and Witchstalker (50.8%) are merely fine. Ferocity of the Hunt at 42.9% confirms the thin theme.

pairs.experts: Both shows see a broad spells deck with Clash of Elements and Saheeli, Jewel of Avishkar as glue. Limited Resources warns to commit to either red aggro or blue control, and is wary of prowess as a main plan.
pairs.sim: UR is middling at 50.5% on a 5% share. Clash of Elements (55.9%) and Tetsuko Umezawa, Pursuer (60.6%, graded only C-/D on Level-Ups) shine. Twinned Vision (49.9%) and Unsummon (47.9%) drag.

pairs.experts: This is the empower-Jace-and-Ways shell. Marc calls Kiora of Salt and Sand's 8/8 plan a trap, Limited Resources calls it fragile, and Mind Meanderer is the standout.
pairs.sim: UG sits at 49.9%. Kiora of Salt and Sand wins 48.3%, backing the trap read, and Way of the Mind Sculptor posts 31.7% on a small sample. Way of the Paradox does surprisingly well at 54.1%.

pairs.experts: Both shows describe an attrition and sacrifice deck with Twisted Fates as its standout. Limited Resources likes Edgar, Ancient Bloodlord at B/B-.
pairs.sim: WB is at 49.9% on a 14% share. Thalia (60.7%) and Twisted Fates (57.5%) carry it, while the sacrifice pieces sink: Edgar wins 45.1% and Winter, Tormented Loner 39.1%. Draft it for the removal and bodies, not the sacrifice theme.

pairs.experts: This is a counters-aggro deck with haste enablers. Mabel, Valley Hero (B+ on Limited Resources) and Warrior's Blades were singled out as strong gold cards.
pairs.sim: WR is the most-drafted pair at 15% but wins only 49.5%. Mabel (49.7%), Warrior's Blades (51.3%) and Gallia, the Merrymaker (51.2%) are all average, and Charge the Sanctum is dreadful at 38.7%. That looks like an overcrowded, overrated lane.

pairs.experts: Limited Resources sees this lifegain-and-counters deck as heavily supported, with Bloombrute at A-. Level-Ups agrees it looks pushed but warns the lifegain enablers are thinner than they appear.
pairs.sim: WG manages only 49.1%. Its good cards are its bodies: Vigorbloom Vanguard, Greenhouse Propagator and Titanbones each win 56.2%. The lifegain payoffs lag, with Bloombrute at 53.2%, Unflinching Hortimancer at 49.9% and Vigorbloom Charm at 46.5%. Marc's caution looks right.

pairs.experts: This is surveil-flyers tempo. Level-Ups' common/uncommon review called it possibly one of the strongest pairs, and Limited Resources rates its signposts highly.
pairs.sim: WU is only average at 49.1% on a 14% share. Desperate Futurescribe (57.1%) and Fatehold Chronologist (54.0%) deliver, but Fatehold Charm (47.5%) and Surveillance Phantasm (50.2%) do not. Surveil sequencing is skill-intensive, so skilled players may beat this number, though the experts' 'best pair' claim is unproven.

pairs.experts: Level-Ups calls this Theorix deck flexible: good-stuff control, turbo self-mill or threshold beatdown. Luis loves the Paradox Shaper loop, but Level-Ups notes the UB prepared spell doesn't affect the board.
pairs.sim: UB is the clear worst at 45.7% and drafted just 4% of the time. Paradox Shaper wins 41.1%, Theorix Charm 45.0% and Theorix Metamage 49.2%. Bots misplay self-mill, and the small deck count means the number is not definitive. Still, it is too consistent a warning to ignore, so draft UB only if it is flowing.

sim_vs_experts.note: Level-Ups calls it one of the best commons (B-), and Limited Resources has it at C/C+. The sim shows 47.9% over 10,000+ games. Bounce is all about timing, which bots do poorly, so the experts have the better case. Limited Resources' more modest C is the safer expectation.

Limited Resources grades it B and Level-Ups C+, yet the sim has it at 47.5%. Its siblings fare similarly: Vigorbloom Charm (B+/B-) wins 46.5% and Theorix Charm (B/C+) 45.0%. Only Konstrari Charm, which both shows rated weakest, beats average at 53.4%. Bots likely misuse modal instants, so trust the experts on the good charms, but don't first-pick them over bodies and removal.

Marc calls it the best rare (A+) and Alex gives it A, but it wins only 48.3% over 3,300 games. Flash, loot-on-attack and token recursion are exactly the lines bots mishandle, so the experts' case is stronger. Treat the sim as a mild warning rather than a verdict.

Alex rates it the best Way (A-), Marc gives it B+ and Limited Resources B. The sim has it at a flat 50.3%, and bots pass it around pick 9.5. Jace-token management is hard for bots, so the experts likely have it right. Pick it highly but not above premium removal.

Graded C+ by Level-Ups and B/B- by Limited Resources, it posts 59.7% over 20,000 games, the best common in the sim. The sample is huge and the card is simple to play, so the sim has the better case: treat it as a top green common.

Both shows give it C, though Level-Ups said it was possibly underrated. It wins 59.5% over 18,000+ games. A four-toughness flying vigilance body with a prepared spell attached is strong in a grindy format, so side with the sim and take it early.

Level-Ups grades it C-/D+ over fear of it rotting in hand, while Limited Resources gives it B-. The sim shows 59.5%, and its sibling Ghalta the Immovable (D- to C-) posts 57.3%. The data backs Limited Resources: cheap-cast giants are real threats here.

Level-Ups has it at C-/D+ and Limited Resources at C-, calling it outclassed. It wins 56.9% over nearly 19,000 games. Bots may struggle against ward, but a durable 5/5 with a pump in a slow format is a legitimate playable. Don't leave it in the sideboard.

Limited Resources calls it an easily supported A- and Marc gives it C. The sim lands in between at 53.2%, only slightly above average, and WG itself underperforms. That supports Marc's point that lifegain enablers are thinner than they look: good, not a bomb.

Level-Ups has it at D (Marc) and C- (Alex), citing three toughness against cheap removal, while Limited Resources has it at B. It wins 56.2% over 6,500 games. The sim clearly sides with Limited Resources.

advice: Lean green, ideally RG. It is Marc's early pick and the sim's best pair at 53.2%, and its big commons (Bestial Incursion, Greenhouse Propagator, Wrecking Gecko) outperform their grades.
Take the proven uncommons early: Craftwork Crusher, Twisted Fates, Kiora of Fire and Ashes and Thalia, the Survivor. Both experts and sim agree on them.
Prioritize black and red removal. Extended Absence, Multiply by Zero, No Admittance, Fulminous Forte and Wrath of the Bloodmane all beat average, and the format rewards trading up.
Value four-toughness and hard-to-kill bodies. Blossom-Blessed Angel, Titanbones and Tetsuko Umezawa, Pursuer all won far more than their grades suggest in a format that stalls.
Cut cheap pump tricks. Perfected Theory (34.0%), Charge the Sanctum (38.7%), Academic Ascent (43.5%) and Tethermage's Advantage (44.9%) are among the worst performers.

Be skeptical of UB self-mill and sacrifice build-arounds like Paradox Shaper, Winter, Tormented Loner and Edgar, Ancient Bloodlord unless the lane is clearly open. WR is the most-drafted pair yet below average, so don't force it either.
Against Jace tokens, send one evasive or awkward-to-block creature at the token and the rest at the opponent's face, as Level-Ups advises. Switch fully to face when the opponent is low.
Pick up the rare duals mid-pack and count sources for heavy pips. Keep color hosers in the sideboard for best-of-three only.

A two-mana flying pump whose Empower 2 almost cantrips.
A 5/4 flyer for four that makes artifacts on entering and dying and has a late-game pump sink; could even be A+.

Tuned for constructed; slow to produce a Pridemate, offers no defense, and is a bad topdeck, especially on the draw.
Makes a token with every activation, pumps and hastes the team, refills your hand, or one-sided wipes; extremely hard to beat.
A Fireball with meaningful trample upside that's great to reuse with Rescue Girl.

A looter with real combat stats that untaps, useful for threshold and flashback.
Selection is abundant and blue needs combat bodies, though was persuaded upward.
A 1/5 trampler that needs creatures entering to hit hard, which is somewhat win-more.
A 1/5 that only grows conditionally for a turn.
Only a playable in prowess spell decks and unplayable elsewhere.
A below-replacement cantrip only for UR spells decks.
At least it can simply cycle on turn one.
A two-mana 2/3 that empowers Jace two on each land drop is strong, and the ultimate becomes realistic with big empower cards.
Strong for its cheap landfall empower, with the -10 ability almost flavor text.
Likely to be overlooked as clunky six-damage removal, but the +1/+1 counter adds stats to the board and landcycling makes it the second-best of the cycle.
Six-damage removal plus a counter, and it can landcycle.
Big removal plus a counter makes it good even ignoring the landcycling, like Cut In.
A pretty good common flashback card: a 4/4 trampler now and another later for six.
A 4/4 trampler with flashback is a two-for-one that ramp decks can turbo out, and trample kills Jaces.
A really solid card.
A 4/4 trampler with flashback is great card advantage, but Unsummon is a big risk.
A trick that replaces itself, good in prowess decks.
Just okay.
Only for low-curve, front-foot red decks.
A clean two-for-one when attacking, and it pairs with cast-from-exile cards.
A hybrid recursive lifelinker that adds up in value and slots into many archetypes as discard or mill fodder.
The three-mana recursion cost is steep, though lifelink on a white one-drop is unusual.
Recursion with lifelink could matter given how much self-mill there is.
The buyback is expensive and there isn't enough sacrifice synergy; you'll rarely play it.
Three deaths in a turn is a real hoop, though the instant draw-three payoff is strong.
In stalled boards it's plausible for three creatures to die in a turn, especially with sac-removal.
Usually wary of expensive creatures without immediate impact, but expects this to draw a card right away fairly often thanks to enter-and-gain-life effects.
A four-mana 4/4 that draws off life gain, which green-white does constantly, plus a lifelink and trample activation late.
A 4-mana 4/4 that draws on lifegain is great when it sticks, and it can draw immediately on turn five with a prepared spell.
Lifegain enablers are thinner than they look, so you won't reliably draw after untapping.
A 2/4 flying vigilance that also casts Seed Suture is strong, yet still just a solid common.
A four-toughness flying vigilance body that becomes a 3/5 or gives haste-turn value at five mana; possibly underrated.
An instant edict that hits their biggest thing and gains two life.
An instant edict that takes their biggest creature and gains two life; possibly underrated.
A 3/3 vigilance with artifact/enchantment removal is filler in a very synergy-driven set.
Pushed just enough to be a fine curve filler.
A fine but unexciting 3/3 that won't make the cut in an uncommon-heavy format.
A hedge in case Way enchantments are central to the format.
A 3/1 for two that trades and later exiles itself from the graveyard to empower Jace.
An instant-speed Empower 2 from the graveyard; use it after they kill your Jace, not to protect it.
A deathtouch 2/3 for two that deters blocks and returns lands, which reach the graveyard often through milling.
Draw two while pinging both players, good for aggressive red-black but not blue-black.
Hitting both players is slight upside.
Draw-two-and-take-damage cards are never good.
A bellwether for prowess; the haste is weak and these cards have been too slow lately.
Power-crept, and haste doesn't fix it starting too small.
Would be more interesting with trample.
Playable but much worse than its mirror, as the surveil plus rarely hits a noncreature spell, though it triggers surveil payoffs.
Still a banger thanks to card advantage, burn, mana, removal, and a quick ultimate.
An expensive but powerful trick that can end the game as a team pump when you go wide.
Three mana is a lot and you can get blown out using it as a single-target trick, though hybrid helps.
Neither pump mode is worth the mana, though it shows up in some go-wide red aggro decks.
A nice removal spell: a top-or-bottom tuck that costs a mana less than usual and punishes opponents who keep the card on top.
A cheap, unconditional instant that removes any nonland permanent or costs them two damage to keep it.
A cheaper top-or-bottom removal that punishes topping; fits tempo UR.
Strong tempo removal; when it targets your token, don't top it, just take the two.
Needs everything to line up, like copying blue-white prepared spells or a self-mill deck, and the activated ability isn't worth using.
A dream card for decks with many prepared spells, including higher-rarity ones, or turbo self-mill blue-black.
A recurring Cadet that grows other wizards is a fun prowess build-around.
A three-mana 2/2 is a weak start and the chaining engine likely won't work.
Probably the best ping payoff, recurring to build a growing wizard army in a grindier RB.
Slow to start, but it pumps all wizard tokens from multiple sources.
Looks really strong: targeting your own planeswalker makes it hard to blow out, and a high-loyalty Jace can turn it into a two-mana deal-eight.
An instant-speed bite that is great with deathtouch, and Jace can even do the biting.
An instant punch that can use planeswalker loyalty as the damage, which avoids some risk.
A Cancel with a surveil, or a two-mana Counterspell if you can behold a Jace.
Often a two-mana hard counter that empowers Jace; great in a set with strong expensive cards.

grades.said: B (up to A- if well enabled)

takes.take: A seven-mana 7/5 trampler with two modes on entry; the ramp deck will often cast it on turn six, and it would have been a rare a few years ago.
A perfect uncommon payoff: a 7/5 trampler with two of removal, a 2/2, or a card, held back only by heavy colored costs.
Rates it a B in a baseline red-green deck and higher with ramp and card draw; likes that it is hard to splash.
A 7/5 trampler that removes something and adds a card or body at uncommon; it pulls you back from almost any board and effectively ends games.
A red Craterhoof that's castable in this slow format and goes from medium to quite strong with one artifact; B+ range in red-green artifacts.
Needs heavy self-mill pairing and most of the time is an overpriced draw three.
Needs around seven or eight of the weak blue-black prepared mill creatures to work reliably.
A 2/1 prowess trades too easily, and prowess as a main plan is weak.
The graveyard stun ability adds some value.
A weak 2/1, and its graveyard ability is too expensive.
Doesn't come together even in UR prowess.
A well-statted 4/4 flying trampler whose tutor-then-random-discard creates interesting decisions.
One trigger from targeting removal makes it a 3/3 first striker that complicates combat.
A first strike two-drop that grows off targeted spells, including the RB ping.
Forgot the ping targets opponents; would raise it to D+.
Draws easily off tricks and equipment, but a 2/2 first striker is small until it gets a counter.
First strike plus draw off prepared spells and tricks; great with the deathtouch aura.
Solid with targeting synergy.
Mostly a 1/2 that mills three and eventually grows, playable but unexciting.
The early mill has a good chance to hit something useful and it grows later.
A fine 3/2 flying haste for four; recursion needs a sac outlet since it only checks at beginning of combat.
A four-mana 3/4 flyer that pumps another attacker each combat, or gives it a permanent counter after a scry or surveil; a pretty good aggressive WU payoff.
Four-mana flyer that pumps your whole team on every scry or surveil and wins fast if it sticks, though flash matters less since most surveils come from main-phase Jace activations.
Nearly always enters untapped, making it better than the common duals and a fine mid-pack pick.
A four-mana 3/4 flyer that pumps a teammate each combat and grows it with counters once you have scried or surveilled.
A four-toughness flyer that dodges common removal and can grow a creature permanently on its first turn with a Jace token around; better than some rares.
Has immediate and lasting impact, and a 3/4 flyer for four is fine on its own.
Bouncing big tokens feels great, but he agreed it's noticeably worse than typical bounce creatures.
A double-blue functional 1/1 that can't hit expensive cards, fitting best in tempo decks.
A flash 3/2 with tap, untap, or loot modes is a fine filler.
Flexible flash filler.
Filler outside of the Splinter Twin combo.
Often just a vanilla 5/5 flyer, but with artifact token makers like the red-green hybrid uncommon it can churn out dragons.
The unblockable effect is usually weak, but it is good at killing Jaces.
A weak two-drop; paying mana for the unblockable ability kills it.
Only fills a two-drop gap.
A really good WB attrition gold card that gains life on deaths and turns sacrifices into counters and menace.
A hard-to-block two-mana 2/3 with an instant-speed sac outlet that fits both white-black and green-white.
Sacrificing your board is not great on its own, but there is enough support to make it fine.
A good-rate two-drop that touches lifegain, counters, and sacrifice, with a threat of activation, though menace is awkward on it.
A flash 4/4 that ambushes attackers and becomes a 6/6 if you pass without casting spells.
Only a bit better than a vanilla five-mana 4/4 flash.

A one-drop that later grows something and gains a life, a flexible enabler for life-gain and counters.

Effectively a nine-mana card that doesn't reliably win when cast, and opponents can sac lands to ward and see it coming.
A late pick for heartwood ramp decks lacking top end, since a 12/12 is hard to kill and it doubles as a weak ramp spell.
Gaining even one life lets it surveil and pull back lands, which is solid value.
Pretty good but not a bomb, since lifegain comes in small amounts.

A strong color hoser against black or green, not maindeckable.

Repeated surveils and a drain, only for surveil, threshold, or prowess decks.

Great on turn one but a poor top deck; rewards skilled players who manipulate their library.
Swingy seven-drop that works best with a planeswalker or empower-Jace support to keep the copies, and can target either player.

Flexible instant that draws a card plus empowers Jace, bounces a threat, or wins combat with +1/+2, so it is good ahead and decent behind.
Its broad modes (cantrip plus Empower Jace 2, tempo bounce, or a team pump that closes games with flyers) fit WU well and could creep into B-.
